reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / IDSA
clinicalPearls: Usually arises from haematogenous seeding of the vertebral body, with the lumbar spine most commonly affected
New or worsening back pain, often unremitting and worse at night, with or without fever should prompt consideration, especially with a recent bacteraemia
Staphylococcus aureus is the most frequent pathogen; consider Gram-negatives with urinary sources and Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Pott's disease) in endemic or chronic presentations
Risk factors include diabetes, injecting drug use, indwelling vascular catheters, recent bacteraemia, endocarditis, and immunosuppression
MRI with contrast is the imaging investigation of choice for early and accurate diagnosis and for detecting epidural extension
Obtaining a microbiological diagnosis, by blood cultures or image-guided biopsy, before starting antibiotics is important unless the patient is septic
Management principles are prolonged targeted antibiotic therapy guided by culture, with surgery reserved for neurological compromise, instability, or failure of medical treatment
Screen for infective endocarditis and other seeding foci when S. aureus bacteraemia is present
reference.pathophysiology: Pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis typically begins when bacteria lodge in the vascular end-plate region of a vertebral body via haematogenous spread from a distant focus. Infection then spreads across the relatively avascular intervertebral disc to involve the adjacent vertebra, producing the characteristic pattern of spondylodiscitis. Progressive infection can form paravertebral or epidural abscesses, erode bone leading to vertebral collapse and deformity, and compress neural structures. Less commonly infection reaches the spine by contiguous spread or direct inoculation from surgery or trauma.
infectionMimics: Malignant infiltration of the vertebral body
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the spine with contrast as the primary imaging test
Blood cultures and inflammatory markers (ESR and CRP) which are useful for diagnosis and monitoring
Image-guided or open biopsy for microbiological and, where relevant, histological diagnosis
Echocardiography to exclude endocarditis when S. aureus or other typical organisms are isolated
Investigations for tuberculosis or brucellosis when the clinical picture is subacute or endemic
redFlags: New neurological deficit, radicular weakness, or bladder or bowel dysfunction suggesting epidural abscess with cord or cauda equina compression requiring emergency imaging and surgery
Signs of spinal instability or progressive vertebral collapse
Sepsis or endocarditis complicating the infection
Rapidly progressive, unremitting, or nocturnal back pain in an at-risk patient
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis and appropriate prolonged antibiotics most patients recover, but delayed treatment or epidural abscess with cord compression can leave permanent neurological deficits; relapse is more likely with inadequate therapy duration or unaddressed source.
pitfalls: Starting antibiotics before securing a microbiological diagnosis in a stable patient, obscuring the causative organism
Attributing persistent back pain to mechanical causes and delaying MRI
Missing an associated epidural abscess or endocarditis
Treating for too short a duration and precipitating relapse
management: Obtain a microbiological diagnosis by blood cultures and image-guided biopsy before starting antibiotics, unless the patient is septic

Give targeted prolonged antibiotic therapy with antistaphylococcal cover for Staphylococcus aureus, tailored cover for Gram-negative or brucella sources, and a multidrug antituberculous regimen for Pott's disease
Pursue source control, including excluding and treating endocarditis and removing infected vascular catheters
Refer for surgical decompression and stabilisation for neurological deficit, epidural abscess with cord compression, spinal instability or failure of medical therapy
Provide supportive care with analgesia, spinal bracing and graded mobilisation
Monitor response with serial inflammatory markers, clinical review and repeat imaging
Optimise predisposing factors such as glycaemic control in diabetes and support for injecting drug use
